name: Cool Earth (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result at the defaults. The cash's value to the communities (97%) split by note 8's programme spending (Peru 76%, Papua New Guinea 16%, Cameroon 6%; the small grant to Go Conscious Earth spread pro rata); the forest's carbon and pandemic risk (3%) spread by world population.
summary: Cool Earth funds Indigenous and local communities in Peru, Papua New Guinea and Cameroon to keep their rainforest standing, mostly with cash given directly to households and community committees, plus data, training and fire prevention. We model all of its programme spending in the year to 31 January 2026 ($4.3 million) in two branches: the forest the support keeps from clearing (a small cut in pandemic risk, and its carbon), and the value of the cash (about £1.2 million) to the people who get it. The result is about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000: over nine tenths of it is the cash itself, valued like a cash transfer to some of the poorest people in Peru and Papua New Guinea. The forest's part is small and rests on a judgment of how much clearing the support prevents; both branches take the missing-data discount, since neither is measured against a comparison.

sections.title: Cost

sections.title: Reach

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.explainer: Cool Earth's whole programme spending in its year to 31 January 2026 (February 2025 to January 2026), with the 70% of support costs the accounts allocate to programmes. Note 8 splits it by country: the Peru hub (its nine partnerships, the basic income pilot, fire prevention and the start of the Colombia pilot), the Papua New Guinea hub (five partnerships), a grant to CCREAD in Cameroon and a grant to Go Conscious Earth. All four are community forest partnerships: cash, data and training for people who keep their forest standing, so they are one model with two branches (the forest kept, and the cash's value to the people who get it).

rows.label: Hectares of rainforest in Cool Earth's partnerships in the year
rows.explainer: The forest of the communities Cool Earth supported in the year, in Peru (most of it, in Asháninka and other Indigenous territories), Papua New Guinea and Cameroon: a stock that the year's support keeps under the communities' control, not land newly protected. An ongoing programme's yearly flow is one year of that forest's protection against one year's cost (Convention 3), so years_protected is 1. Cool Earth's own count; no independent register.

rows.label: Livelihoods: cash reaching households and community committees in the year, pounds

source.title: Cool Earth Action, Trustees' report and audited financial statements for the year ended 31 January 2026 (text of the accounts filed with the Charity Commission, charity 1117978; audited by RRL LLP)
source.page: p. 16, Income and Fundraising; notes 7-10, pp. 35-37; note 15, p. 40
source.quote: In 2025, Cool Earth spent over £3.2m on programmatic work, including £2m given directly to communities living in rainforest.

rows.explainer: Unconditional cash to households (the basic income pilot in Peru, household transfers in Papua New Guinea, emergency cash after floods and fires) and grants to the communities' own committees, which spend them on food, health posts, school costs and teachers, water tanks and crops (trustees' report, Programmes, Goal 1). Cool Earth's £2m can't all be cash: it matches the 61% of programme spending the report calls locally directed (£1.99m), which includes the hubs' local staff. The accounts give £2,243,454 of activities run directly in Peru and Papua New Guinea (note 8); taking out the programmes' own staff (£713,011: note 10's £1,641,262 of staff costs less note 9's £928,251 in support and governance) and the restricted projects that aren't cash (forest research, cacao, fish farming, solar lighting: about £0.36m, note 15) leaves about £1.17m; the grants to CCREAD and Go Conscious Earth (£0.19m) pass some cash on too, and data and equipment take some. The ceiling is the programmes' direct costs less their staff, about £1.72m (note 7's £2,437,731 less £713,011). Our estimate £1.2m (£0.8m-£1.72m).

rows.label: Livelihoods: cash given directly, US dollars
rows.explainer: At the IRS's 2025 average rate, the year the cash was given.

rows.label: Livelihoods: people in the communities who share the year's cash
rows.explainer: Cool Earth counts 103,000 Indigenous people supported now (Impact Report 2025/6, p. 15), the high end, and 59,000 with better access to data, training and tools (p. 8); the cash reaches fewer: its 2022 strategy lists six Peruvian and three Papua New Guinean partnership communities at the time, since grown to nine and five partnerships (trustees' report, p. 11), some of them federations of many villages. Our judgment 40,000 (10,000-103,000). The result hardly depends on it: spread over fewer people the same cash raises each one's consumption more, and the log of consumption gained is close to the cash over consumption either way.

rows.label: Health: people whose air, water, food or disease exposure the protection changes
rows.explainer: 0: the health posts, water tanks and medicine the communities buy with the cash are counted in the cash's value to them (the livelihoods branch), not again here.

rows.label: Wellbeing: people who visit or live with the protected nature
rows.explainer: 0: the partnerships' forests are remote Indigenous territories with no visitors to count; the communities' own wellbeing from their forest is in the livelihoods branch.

rows.label: Wild animals: animal-years whose welfare the protection changes
rows.explainer: 0: Cool Earth claims no welfare effect on wild animals, and more animals alive is not by itself a gain (conservation family); the sign is unknown.

rows.label: Years of protection one year's spending buys
rows.explainer: One: the year's cash, data and training keep the year's partnerships going; the next year's spending buys the next year (Convention 3: an ongoing programme's yearly flow against one year's cost). Whether the forest kept this year is kept for good is the permanence row below, not more years here.

rows.label: Years of protection, discounted
rows.explainer: Every year of protection, and the wait before it, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Climate: years until the tonnes are avoided
rows.explainer: The cash and support arrive through the year and the clearing they prevent would have happened through the same year: half a year on average (0-1).

rows.label: Forest: share of comparable community forest lost a year without the support
rows.explainer: The loss the support works against, on Indigenous and community land like the partnerships' without Cool Earth. Anchors: Cool Earth's own briefing (p. 11) gives 0.14% a year for Indigenous and local communities' forests in the Amazon on average, our best guess, and 1.34% a year in 2019-2023 for the 23.5 million most at-risk hectares of Indigenous-owned Amazon forest. Cool Earth's long-standing partnerships lose about 0.05% a year with the support (99% standing since 2007); with the 30% the support prevents (for_counterfactual_adj) that implies a baseline near 0.07%, the low end. The partnerships sit on active frontiers (coca and settlers along Peru's Ene river, a logging company camped by the Papua New Guinea villages: trustees' report, p. 10), so the high end is 0.5% a year, well below the most at-risk land's rate, which the partnerships' own record rules out.

rows.label: Forest: share of the year's avoided loss that stays standing for good
rows.explainer: A year's support delays clearing; some of the forest kept would be cleared in a later year anyway, if the threat outlasts the support. Anchors: Cool Earth's partnerships have kept their forest for up to 18 years (99% standing since 2007, trustees' report, Objectives and activities), which argues for most of it lasting; but logging offers and coca recur, and studies of payments for forest find some of the effect fades after payments stop. Our judgment half (20-90%). One question only: whether the support prevents the year's clearing at all is the counterfactual row.

rows.label: Forest: CO₂ released per hectare of tropical forest lost
rows.explainer: The tropics' average, 2.4 billion tonnes over 3.7 million hectares lost in 2023 (about {{row:tco2_per_ha_lost}} tonnes a hectare; World Resources Institute, the shared figures every forest model reads). Cool Earth says its Peru partnerships are among the most carbon-dense forests (p. 10), which would raise it; its own briefing uses 118 tonnes of carbon a hectare (about 430 t CO₂), which would lower it. Both are inside evidence_adj.

rows.label: Climate: tonnes of CO₂e a year a protected hectare keeps out of the air
rows.explainer: The emissions a hectare would release a year without the support, kept for good: loss rate × permanence × CO₂ per hectare lost. The share the support prevents is not in this figure: it is the forest branch's counterfactual row, so a hectare that would be lost anyway is counted once (conservation family pitfall).

rows.label: Forest: hectares a year at risk that would be lost for good
rows.explainer: The partnerships' forest × the loss rate × the share that would stay lost: about 600 hectares at the best guesses, before the support's effect (for_counterfactual_adj).

rows.label: Forest: tonnes of CO₂ at risk over the years counted (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The hectares × the tonnes a hectare would release a year × the discounted year of protection.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: deaths if the catastrophe happens
rows.explainer: The shared figure: WHO's 14.9 million excess deaths in 2020-2021, the pandemic the yearly chance below is defined by.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic
rows.explainer: The shared figure (Marani et al. 2021): about {{row:pandemic_annual_probability}} a year.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of new diseases whose emergence land-use change drove
rows.explainer: The shared figure (IPBES 2020): more than {{row:land_use_share_of_emergence}} of new diseases since 1960.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of the land-use risk that scales with tropical forest loss
rows.explainer: The shared judgment (facts/catastrophe.json): half of the land-use risk scales with tropical forest loss (10-100%), anchored on Allen et al. (2017). No study has measured this dose.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: fall in the yearly pandemic chance per hectare of tropical forest kept
rows.explainer: The land-use share of new diseases × the share of it that scales with tropical forest loss × the yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic, per hectare of the tropics' yearly loss: the risk falls in proportion to the forest kept. The least grounded number here.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: fall in the catastrophe's yearly probability from the year's work
rows.explainer: The forest kept for good after the branch's adjustments × the risk per hectare: the fall in the yearly chance of a COVID-scale pandemic, about one in ten million. For reading and the bounds check; for_uov_pandemic carries it.

rows.label: Share of the catastrophe's deaths that are of children under five
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: mostly older people died, few young children.

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: school-age children were the least affected.

rows.label: Of the catastrophe's deaths at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: The shared judgment for a COVID-scale pandemic: about 15% of adult excess deaths were under 50; the rest are valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: A catastrophe's deaths are valued like every death on the site, by age band × your value of a life; no premium for their number.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: share of every later year's healthy life the catastrophe would take
rows.explainer: The shared judgment: 0, the world recovers from a COVID-scale pandemic; its deaths are counted above.

rows.label: Discounted future years of healthy life per person of the long-run population, if the future ends now
rows.explainer: The site's one count of future generations (docs/normalization.md 2.19): the healthy years of people not yet born, discounted for ever at the shared rate. People alive now die in the catastrophe and are counted as deaths, so this stream rises from nothing to the long-run population over one lifetime (@catastrophe.life_expectancy_now) and then runs on: about 8 years at the default 4%, about 960 at the 0.1% floor. Fixed; don't edit.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: pandemic deaths averted, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: The forest kept for good × the risk cut per hectare × the discounted year × the pandemic's deaths × the value of a death.

rows.label: Catastrophic risk: future years of healthy life kept, discounted
rows.formula: for_lasting_loss_ha_per_year * risk_per_ha_year * protection_years * for_credit * future_share_lost * @catastrophe.world_population_long_run * future_years_per_person
rows.explainer: Every later year's healthy life the pandemic would take from people not yet born, discounted for ever at the shared rate; 0 at the best guess (future_share_lost). Already credited by the forest branch.

rows.label: Suffering of the farmed animals the people of that future would eat, in healthy years
rows.explainer: A future kept is also every animal raised to feed it: each future person-year at the suffering of the animals an average person eats in a year today (docs/normalization.md 2.25). Suffering always counts, whatever lives that never start count; the farmed animals' own good days count where you set them to. Held at today's diet: no forecast of what people will eat is used.

rows.label: Health: DALYs averted per person per year
rows.explainer: Not reached: health_people is 0.

rows.label: Livelihoods: Peru's household-survey mean consumption per person, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: The household-survey mean (World Bank PIP) in 2024 US$ at market prices: about $3,000 a year. Peru gets three quarters of the programme spending (note 8).

rows.label: Livelihoods: partner communities' consumption as a share of Peru's survey mean
rows.explainer: Indigenous Amazonian communities are among Peru's poorest, living largely from their own crops, fish and forest with little cash income; Papua New Guinea's rural villages (a sixth of the spending) are poorer than Peru's average too. The poorest fifth in a country's survey consume about 40% of its mean, and remote Amazonian households less. Our judgment 35% (20-60%), about $1,000 a person a year.

rows.label: Livelihoods: consumption per person a year in the partner communities, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: In US$ at market prices, the same basis as the cash, so no PPP factor is needed (2025 cash against 2024 prices; the year's US inflation, under 3%, is inside the share's range).

rows.label: Livelihoods: ln(consumption) gain per person per year
rows.explainer: The year's cash on the site's one log-consumption scale: spent within the year (paid monthly, or by the committees over the year), so the gain is ln(1 + cash per person ÷ a year's consumption): about 4% at the best guesses. Whatever is invested (crops, gardens) and its returns are in the branch's unmodelled share.

rows.label: Livelihoods: the cash's value, in units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: People × the year's gain in log consumption × the shared value of a doubled consumption. One year: the cash is the year's, not a protection that lasts.

rows.label: Wellbeing: life satisfaction gained per person per year (points, 0-10)
rows.explainer: Not reached: nature_people is 0.

rows.label: Wild animals: days of disabling pain spared per animal-year (negative if more)
rows.explainer: Not reached: wild_animal_years is 0.

rows.label: Wild animals: days of pain spared (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: 0: no wild-animal welfare effect is counted (wild_animal_years is 0).

rows.label: Wild animals: chicken-equivalent pain days
rows.explainer: 0: the species step for wild animals, not reached here (wild_animal_years is 0).

rows.label: Forest: evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: How far to trust the forest chain: the effect is anchored on a randomised trial of conditional payments in Uganda, applied to unconditional cash and support in the Amazon and Papua New Guinea (×0.85); the loss rate and CO₂ per hectare are regional and tropical averages, not the partnerships' own (×0.85). Together 0.7 (0.4-1).

rows.label: Forest: share of the at-risk loss the support prevents
rows.explainer: What the cash, data and training change. Anchors: in the one randomised trial, Jayachandran et al. (Science, 2017), paying Ugandan forest owners to keep their trees cut the loss by about half over two years (tree cover fell 4.2% in paid villages against 9.1% in the others); those payments were conditional and monitored, Cool Earth's mostly unconditional (forest agreements with the committees, monitoring by the communities' own satellites and patrols). Unconditional income can also raise clearing (Alix-Garcia et al. 2013 on Mexico's cash transfers) or lower it (Ferraro and Simorangkir 2020 on Indonesia's). Indigenous territories already keep their forest far better than other land (Sze et al. 2022: 2.5 times less loss), and that is in the baseline, not Cool Earth's credit. Cool Earth's own satellite comparison finds its partnerships losing forest three times more slowly than comparable areas, mostly not Indigenous-managed (2022 strategy, p. 7); against the 2.5 times Indigenous land shows anyway, that leaves about 17% of the loss for the support itself, an observational cross-check. Our judgment 30% (5-60%), below the conditional trial's half and above the cross-check.

rows.label: Forest: Cool Earth's share of the resources behind the forest kept
rows.explainer: The communities' own patrols, monitoring and refusals of loggers, their federations (CARE, ONAMIAP, OMIAASEC), partners such as CCREAD, and other funders of the same territories (government titling and Peru's national forest conservation programme, which pays some Indigenous communities to keep forest) work beside Cool Earth's money. Convention 2: the communities' unpaid time is part of the resources. Our judgment 70% (40-100%): Cool Earth is the main outside funder of its partnerships.

rows.label: Forest: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Cash reaches the communities (Cool Earth's own reports; the trustees' report gives 61% of programme spending as locally directed), but elite capture has happened (Gadaisu, Papua New Guinea, 2018: the 2022 strategy, p. 7) and partnerships take 12-18 months to start. 90% (70-100%).

rows.label: Forest: benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Negative: leakage, clearing pushed onto forest outside the partnerships (studies of protected areas find from none to about 40% of the avoided loss displaced; the Uganda trial found none). Positive: Cool Earth's policy work for climate finance paid directly to forest communities, wildfire prevention in CARE's territory (fires fell from 25 in 2023 to none in 2025), biodiversity and water. Net −5% (−35% to +20%).

rows.label: Forest: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: Cool Earth counts its hectares and measures loss inside its partnerships by satellite, and its one comparison (three times less loss than comparable areas, 2022 strategy p. 7) is against land not managed by Indigenous communities, so it can't separate the support's effect from the communities' own, as the strategy itself says; the effect here is from research on other programmes. The shared missing-data discount (Convention 12).

rows.label: Forest: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The forest branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Forest: adjustments and unmodelled effects
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments × (1 + its unmodelled effects). A unit cost: no next-dollar factor (Convention 11).

rows.label: Livelihoods: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: Cash raises consumption by about what is given (the cash-transfer trials behind the site's cash benchmark); part of it here is spent by the committees on health posts, teachers and water tanks, valued as if the households had spent it, which may over- or understate it. 0.9 (0.6-1).

rows.label: Livelihoods: share of the cash that wouldn't have come anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the cash is Cool Earth's own and no government or other funder would have given these communities the same; Peru's national cash transfer reaches few of them. Whether the cash crowds out the communities' own earnings is in the delivery and unmodelled rows.

rows.label: Livelihoods: Cool Earth's share of the resources behind the cash
rows.explainer: 1: the cash is Cool Earth's, delivered by its own hubs and partners whose costs are in the programme spending.

rows.label: Livelihoods: delivery adjustment
rows.explainer: Share of the cash that reaches people as intended: bank and transfer fees, elite capture (Gadaisu 2018) and slow starts. 90% (70-100%), as for the forest branch.

rows.label: Livelihoods: benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Positive: returns on cash invested in crops and gardens, and health from the health posts and water tanks beyond their cost (child deaths averted and spillovers to others are their own rows below). Negative: income from loggers or settlers forgone where the forest is kept (small: the branch's forest is a few hundred hectares a year). Net +5% (−10% to +25%).

rows.label: Livelihoods: deaths averted by the cash, as a share of its consumption value (at the default value of a life)
rows.explainer: The cash-income recipe's mortality ratio. Anchor: GiveWell's November 2024 GiveDirectly analysis values the deaths cash averts (under-five deaths cut by 45% × 0.5 for internal validity, adult deaths half as much again) at about a quarter of the consumption value at Kenya's under-five mortality of about 5%, the high end. The partner communities' under-five mortality is lower, about 3% (our judgment: Peru's Amazonian Indigenous peoples well above Peru's national rate, Papua New Guinea's rural villages near Kenya's), and much of the cash goes to committees rather than mothers: our judgment 12% (4-25%); the low end is GiveWell's older supplemental +4% (@givewell_common.child_mortality_effects).

rows.label: Livelihoods: deaths averted by the cash, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: The ratio × your value of a life, so these deaths move with it like every death on the site.

rows.label: Livelihoods: gains to others from the cash spent locally, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: A side effect: cash spent in the communities' few shops and markets raises traders' and producers' incomes, and committee spending (teachers, health posts) pays local people. The shared figure for cash spent locally, +{{row:liv_spillover_share}} (0 to +40%).

rows.label: Livelihoods: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: the cash given is Cool Earth's own figure, but the people who share it are a judgment and much of it is given to committees, unlike the household transfers the trials measure. The shared missing-data discount (Convention 12).

rows.label: Livelihoods: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The livelihoods branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Livelihoods: adjustments and unmodelled effects
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments × (1 + its unmodelled effects, the child deaths averted and the spillovers to others).

rows.label: Healthy years per tonne at your settings (for the averages only)
rows.explainer: Read off the bridge rows, only to weight the branch averages below; nothing on the path reads it.

rows.label: Healthy years per unit of value at your settings (for the averages only)
rows.explainer: Read off the bridge rows, only to weight the branch averages below; nothing on the path reads it.

rows.label: Forest: healthy years before adjustments
rows.explainer: The branch's outcomes before its adjustments, in healthy years: its weight in the averages below.

rows.label: Livelihoods: healthy years before adjustments
rows.explainer: The branch's outcome before its adjustments, in healthy years: its weight in the averages below.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: weighted average of the branches
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by the branch's healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: Counterfactual: weighted average of the branches
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by the branch's healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: Cool Earth's share of the resources: weighted average of the branches
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by the branch's healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by the branch's healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: Delivery: weighted average of the branches
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by the branch's healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: 1: the other resources behind the forest are in the forest branch's attribution share, so leverage isn't counted again, and a gift to Cool Earth doesn't obviously displace other funders of these communities. Range 0.85-1.1. Applied to both branches.

rows.label: Missing-data discount: weighted average of the branches
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by the branch's healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: All adjustments combined: weighted average of the branches
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by the branch's healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: Effects not modelled: weighted average of the branches
rows.explainer: Outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only: each branch applies its own row (Convention 4), weighted by the branch's healthy years before adjustments.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes that are methane
rows.explainer: 0: the tonnes are land carbon, CO₂ from forest kept standing; no methane is counted (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fossil fuel near people
rows.explainer: 0: land carbon carries no fossil-fuel smoke (conservation family); the partnerships' forest is kept from clearing and logging, not burned for fuel near cities.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of this fuel, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: Not reached: fuel_share is 0.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: Read by the tonnes' bridge, as by the tco2e unit's conversion.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly (none here)
rows.explainer: Deaths a source counts directly beside the tonnes: none. Clearing fires' smoke is small next to the tonnes and left out (conservation family).

rows.label: Livelihoods and catastrophic risk, in GiveWell units of value (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Each branch's units of value × that branch's credit: the pandemic risk the forest kept cuts, and the cash's value to the communities.

rows.label: Livelihoods and catastrophic risk, in healthy years
rows.explainer: The bridge from UoV into healthy years (docs/normalization.md 2.6): fixed, don't edit.

rows.label: Wellbeing from nature, in wellbeing-adjusted life years (before adjustments)
